tips.text: The design of Bus Stop signs in Latvia is a blue background with a white square, inside the white square is a bus with 5 windows. The design is the same in Estonia and Lithuania, the main difference in Latvia however is that it has 5 windows, while the other 2 have 4 windows on their Bus Stop signs. Important: 5 windows

The design of Bus Stop signs in Lithuania and Estonia is a blue background with a white square, inside the white square is a bus with 4 windows. The design in Latvia has 5 windows instead of 4. Important: 4 windows
Warning signs in Lithuania have a thin red border surrounded by a narrow white outline. Important: a thin red border
Latvian warning signs have a thick red border with a thin white outline. Important: thick red border
Estonian warning signs have a thin red border with no white outline, extending to the edge of the sign. Important: without white outline

Lithuanian kilometer markers are typically blue and shaped like an open book or a check mark. A green variant can also be found, although it is much less common. Important: marker with a check mark shape
Latvian kilometer markers are typically blue, flat, single-sided, and mounted parallel to the road. Important: marker is parallel to the road
Like those in the other Baltic countries, Estonian kilometer markers are typically blue. They are rectangular and mounted perpendicular to the road. Important: Marker is perpendicular to the road

Latvian directional signs have a blue background with white text and a white outline. Very important is that while the design is similar to Estonia and Lithuania, the back part of the arrowhead is not just one straight line, but instead looks like this. Important: The arrow tip is curved

Lithuanian and Estonia directional signs have a blue background with white text and a white outline. The back edge of the arrowhead must form a straight line. In Latvia, it does not. Important: The arrow tip is straight

- Shape and color: Square light-blue background with white triangle - Figure: Black with thick torso. 4 separate parts - head, one leg, one arm and the rest of the body - Zebra stripes: 3 black stripes Important: simplified pedestrian figure with three stripes

The Estonian pedestrian crossing sign has three zebra stripes and a more detailed pedestrian figure. Lithuania also uses three zebra stripes, but the pedestrian figure is more stylized. - Shape and color: Square blue background with white triangle - Figure: Black realistic person. 2 arms and one hand is not visible. No separate parts - Zebra stripes: 3 black thick stripes Important: A detailed pedestrian figure with three stripes.

Latvia is unique among the Baltic countries for using five zebra stripes on its pedestrian crossing sign. - Shape and color: Square blue background with white triangle - Figure: Black with very long legs. 3 separate parts - head, one leg and the rest of the body Important: Zebra stripes: 5 black stripes
The Lithuanian word for street is "gatve" which is very often abbreviated as "g."
The Latvian word for street is "iela".
Estonia's country code top-level domain is .ee.
Latvia's country code top-level domain is .lv.
Lithuania's country code top-level domain is .lt.

One of the most common utility poles in Estonia has a distinctive trident-like shape. While the number of insulators may vary, the overall trident form remains the same. Important: trident-like shape with a central vertical steel beam
Utility poles with long crossarms featuring curved end brackets are unique to Estonia.

Latvian utility poles are easily recognized by their alternating hook-shaped insulators at the top. These hooked utility poles can be found in both single and double configurations. Important: hook-shaped insulators Note:This design is most common in Latvia, although it can occasionally be seen in the other Baltic countries and elsewhere in Europe.

Lithuania features a wide variety of utility pole tops. One common design has a trident-like shape. Unlike its Estonian counterpart, the central insulators are mounted directly on the pole instead of on a steel beam. The number of insulators on this type of pole may vary. Important: Central insulators are pole-mounted. Note: also found in other countries, but much less common.

Another recognizable Lithuanian utility pole features short crossarms. The number of crossarms may vary, but their short length is the defining characteristic. Important: short crossarms Note: also found in other countries, but much less common.

This pole top, featuring a short crossarm with rounded end elements, is characteristic of Lithuania. Short crossarm with rounded ends Note: Similar designs exist in some post-Soviet countries, but they are far less common.

White cylinder with flat top Reflector position: Main reflector – white (or orange/yellow) vertically oriented rectangle. On the rear side, two white (or orange/yellow) circles. Both side in a black diagonal frame Important: round cross-section
Classic European wedge bollard with orange front rectangle reflector and white back. Important: wedge-shaped cross-section

Flat rectangular white panel (plank-like). Latvian bollard appears almost 2D when viewed from the side, with a flat top and flat faces. Important: flat bollard, sometimes with numbers Reflector: - Front reflector – white (most common) or yellow (intersections, bridges and etc) rectangle inside the black diagonal stripe. - On the rear side, two small circular white reflectors Unique numbers: A large black digit is usually printed below the front reflector. The number represents the distance marker toward the next kilometer post (in hundreds of meters)

This kind of “cap” on top of utility poles is not found in Lithuania. Be careful, though - it is quite common not only in the Baltic countries, but also across Northern Europe. Pole caps are not found in Lithuania

Latvian chevrons have a white background with red arrows, just like in Lithuania. Be careful—Estonia uses the opposite design: white arrows on a red background! - Background: White - Arrows: Bold red Note: This chevron can have one or multiple arrows.

Estonia is unique among the Baltic countries with its red chevrons featuring white arrows. Lithuania and Latvia use the opposite design: white chevrons with red arrows. Background: Red Arrows: White Note: this type of chevron can have a different number of arrows.

Some chevrons in Lithuania feature a thin red border. - Background: White - Arrows: Bold red Important: red border Note: But besides these types of chevrons, the country also commonly has regular ones without the thin red border.
Õ is exclusive to the Estonian alphabet and cannot be found in the alphabets of Latvia or Lithuania. A visually similar letter is used in Portuguese.
Ā Ē Ī - Unique Latvian Vowels with a macron (horizontal stripe)

tips.section: Unique Consonants of the Latvian language
tips.text: Ģ, Ķ, Ļ, and Ņ are unique Latvian letters that represent softened (palatalized) consonants. They have no direct equivalents in English and are one of the defining features of the Latvian alphabet.
Ė is a unique letter of the Lithuanian alphabet, commonly found on street signs and road signs across Lithuania.
Ą, Ę, Į, and Ų are distinctive Lithuanian letters with ogoneks. They are commonly seen on street names and road signs throughout Lithuania.
Lithuania is the only Baltic country to use orange guardrail reflectors. Their reverse side is white. Orange reflectors Note: Estonia has no guardrail reflectors, while Latvia uses red or white ones.
These blue-and-white reflective wraps on road signs are very common in Estonia. Blue-and-white reflective wraps Note: They are also commonly found in Finland and Sweden.
Oval blue house numbers are common in Estonia. They are rare elsewhere in the Baltics but can also be found in Russia.
Latvian house numbers are commonly tall, rectangular, and available in various colors. Note: They are rarely found in Estonia or Lithuania.
The historical flag of Lithuania, known as the Vytis, features a mounted knight on a dark red background. It can occasionally be seen on both private and public buildings.

The Estonian word for street is "tänav", which is usually abbreviated as "tn" A lot of streets do not have the suffix however. Note: besides "tänav", "tee" is also commonly found on Estonian street signs.
